ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Informed consent was obtained in accordance with the MU Institutional Review Board.

Subjects are then asked to recall and report (often verbally) either all of the items in order of list presentation for serial recall, as many items in any order for free recall, and a single or limited number of items relative to a provided list item (cue) for cued recall.

Building on those ideas, Guitard and Saint-Aubin (2022; also see Guitard et al., 2020) combined dual-task procedures with whether or not subjects were provided foreknowledge about the serial recall direction prior to encoding.
table.formatted: Building on those ideas, Guitard and Saint-Aubin (2022; also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Guitard et al., 2020)</ref> combined dual-task procedures with whether or not subjects were provided foreknowledge about the serial recall direction prior to encoding.

table.text: After studying lists of seven to nine words, our subjects completed an immediate cued recall task in which one word from the list was presented as a cue along with right-or left-ward symbols respectively indicating that the next or previous two list words should be reported.

Finally, and not unrelated to the previous two features, we employed an extended (5-second) deliberation period with our cued recall task, ensuring that subjects had adequate time to actively engage in retrieval processing prior to being signaled to verbally report.
Informed consent was obtained in accordance with the MU Institutional Review Board.
Data from four subjects were excluded from all analyses: one due to technical errors with the EEG recording, one due to too much artifact in the EEG, and two for abnormal behavioral performance.
Upon arriving at the laboratory, subjects were instructed about and completed practice versions of the experiment's tasks.

The word and symbols were displayed centrally for a 5-s deliberation period, while subjects were asked to search for and continually think about the next two or previous two words relative to the cued position.
A row of five question marks ('?????') was then shown centrally for 4 s, during which subjects were to verbally report the words they recalled.

Subjects were additionally instructed that, in the event that they were unsure about the next or previous two words or their exact order, they should report their best guess(es) or partial information, emphasizing that recalling words from the cued direction was most important.

This epoch length captured the entire 5-s period (0 to 5 s) during which subjects were to deliberate about the adjacent study words, plus a baseline period (-1 to 0 s) and additional temporal padding (1 s in each direction) to accommodate the time-frequency transformation (see below).

Following each study list, subjects were instructed to recall and verbally report two words from the list, either in the forward or backward direction, relative to the position of a provided cue word (see Figure 1a).
table.formatted: Following each study list, subjects were instructed to recall and verbally report two words from the list, either in the forward or backward direction, relative to the position of a provided cue word (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

table.text: If both words could not be recalled, subjects were to report partial information or make their best guess, with the instructions emphasizing the report of words from the cued direction (which was most relevant to the EEG classification analyses).

Given that subjects were instructed to deliberate about retrieval throughout the 5-s period in which the word and direction cues were presented, the classification analyses were initially conducted on the EEG data averaged over this period.
The behavioral results indicated success of the task's primary goal, in that subjects were able to report the desired number of recalled items.

Importantly, considering the current results in the context of these position and lag effects indicated that subjects were able to successfully retrieve memories in both directions and, moreover, did so with equivalent performance across direction.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "Additionally, to highlight the electrodes and frequency bands exhibiting the strongest weights, a standard, critical t-value (t23 = 2.069, p < .05, two-tailed) was used for thresholding."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

We examined 184 columns across 23 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 23 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Subjects are then asked to recall and report (often verbally) either all of the items in order of list presentation for serial recall, as many items in any order for free recall, and a single or limited number of items relative to a provided list item (cue) for cued recall.

Building on those ideas, Guitard and Saint-Aubin (2022; also see Guitard et al., 2020) combined dual-task procedures with whether or not subjects were provided foreknowledge about the serial recall direction prior to encoding.

After studying lists of seven to nine words, our subjects completed an immediate cued recall task in which one word from the list was presented as a cue along with right-or left-ward symbols respectively indicating that the next or previous two list words should be reported.

Finally, and not unrelated to the previous two features, we employed an extended (5-second) deliberation period with our cued recall task, ensuring that subjects had adequate time to actively engage in retrieval processing prior to being signaled to verbally report.
Informed consent was obtained in accordance with the MU Institutional Review Board.
Data from four subjects were excluded from all analyses: one due to technical errors with the EEG recording, one due to too much artifact in the EEG, and two for abnormal behavioral performance.
Upon arriving at the laboratory, subjects were instructed about and completed practice versions of the experiment's tasks.

The word and symbols were displayed centrally for a 5-s deliberation period, while subjects were asked to search for and continually think about the next two or previous two words relative to the cued position.
A row of five question marks ('?????') was then shown centrally for 4 s, during which subjects were to verbally report the words they recalled.

Subjects were additionally instructed that, in the event that they were unsure about the next or previous two words or their exact order, they should report their best guess(es) or partial information, emphasizing that recalling words from the cued direction was most important.

This epoch length captured the entire 5-s period (0 to 5 s) during which subjects were to deliberate about the adjacent study words, plus a baseline period (-1 to 0 s) and additional temporal padding (1 s in each direction) to accommodate the time-frequency transformation (see below).

Following each study list, subjects were instructed to recall and verbally report two words from the list, either in the forward or backward direction, relative to the position of a provided cue word (see Figure 1a).

If both words could not be recalled, subjects were to report partial information or make their best guess, with the instructions emphasizing the report of words from the cued direction (which was most relevant to the EEG classification analyses).

Given that subjects were instructed to deliberate about retrieval throughout the 5-s period in which the word and direction cues were presented, the classification analyses were initially conducted on the EEG data averaged over this period.
The behavioral results indicated success of the task's primary goal, in that subjects were able to report the desired number of recalled items.

Importantly, considering the current results in the context of these position and lag effects indicated that subjects were able to successfully retrieve memories in both directions and, moreover, did so with equivalent performance across direction.

#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **12 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

info.title: Traveling back and forth through time: oscillatory brain patterns distinguish directional cued recall

text.text: • Directional recall was used to test episodic retrieval transitions over time.
• Behavioral performance was equated across direction, minimizing confounds.
• Classic effects of serial position and contiguity were replicated with cued recall.
• Multivariate EEG analysis classified forward and backward recall directions.
• High-frequency (gamma) oscillatory activity distinguished direction conditions.

Association is a hallmark of episodic memory, serving to relate new events to past memories, multiple details coherently into a single episode, and contiguous events to a common spatiotemporal context.

The links between time and memory, in particular, help with organizing our ongoing experiences, can lead to the adoption of search and other strategic processes at the time of retrieval, and are central to the theoretical concept of mental time travel (Tulving, 1985 (Tulving, , 2002;; Wheeler, Stuss, & Tulving, 1997; for related discussions, see Friedman, 1993; Davachi and DuBrow, 2015; Cohn-Sheehy and Ranganath, 2017; Howard, 2017).
text.formatted: The links between time and memory, in particular, help with organizing our ongoing experiences, can lead to the adoption of search and other strategic processes at the time of retrieval, and are central to the theoretical concept of mental time travel <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Tulving, 1985</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Tulving, , 2002;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Wheeler, Stuss, & Tulving, 1997</ref>; for related discussions, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Friedman, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Davachi and DuBrow, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cohn-Sheehy and Ranganath, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Howard, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work on the temporal aspects of episodic memory has taken a variety of approaches, from contrasting past retrieval to future simulation (e.g., Addis et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2012), investigating the phenomenology and neural basis of replaying sequences of memories (e.g., Foster, 2017; Wimmer et al., 2020), and characterizing how a continuous stream of information is segmented into discrete events (e.g., Zacks et al., 2007; Ezzyat and Davachi, 2011; Baldassano et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Recent work on the temporal aspects of episodic memory has taken a variety of approaches, from contrasting past retrieval to future simulation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Addis et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Szpunar et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Schacter et al., 2012)</ref>, investigating the phenomenology and neural basis of replaying sequences of memories (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Foster, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Wimmer et al., 2020)</ref>, and characterizing how a continuous stream of information is segmented into discrete events (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Zacks et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Ezzyat and Davachi, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Baldassano et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Aside from these growing research areas, there is also a long history of studies using classic list-learning paradigms to understand the associations between consecutive events (or items) and how memories are represented across time.

The current study borrows elements from these paradigms to explore how the temporal associations formed at encoding subsequently influence retrieval, with the primary goal of providing novel neural evidence for a distinction between the temporal directions (forward versus backward) of retrieval.
A large body of findings from three experimental psychology procedures have been extensively used to investigate list-based memory: serial, free, and cued recall.
The standard version of each of these procedures involves first presenting subjects with a study (encoding) list usually consisting of about five to 20 successive items (e.g., words).

Subjects are then asked to recall and report (often verbally) either all of the items in order of list presentation for serial recall, as many items in any order for free recall, and a single or limited number of items relative to a provided list item (cue) for cued recall.

Findings across these procedures typically show that items from the beginning and end of the lists are better recalled than those from the middle (primacy and recency effects, respectively; e.g., Deese and Kaufman, 1957; Murdock, 1962; for reviews, see Hurlstone et al., 2014; Lewandowsky and Farrell, 2008).
text.formatted: Findings across these procedures typically show that items from the beginning and end of the lists are better recalled than those from the middle (primacy and recency effects, respectively; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Deese and Kaufman, 1957;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Murdock, 1962</ref>; for reviews, see <ref type="bibr">Hurlstone et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Lewandowsky and Farrell, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the likelihood of recalling a particular item often depends on whether other adjacent items have already been recalled, suggesting the reliance on associations formed across items or with positions (Kahana et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Moreover, the likelihood of recalling a particular item often depends on whether other adjacent items have already been recalled, suggesting the reliance on associations formed across items or with positions <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Kahana et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Because a subset of studies employing each of these paradigms have attempted to understand the basis of forward versus backward transitions across list positions at the time of retrieval, and because elements of those studies are employed in the current study, we further discuss each procedure in turn here.
Some studies of serial recall have manipulated whether the list is to be recalled in the standard, forward order, or instead, in the backward order (i.e., starting with the final item of the list).

Early research of this sort was motivated to test the proposal that recall was largely limited to the direction of encoding (i.e., forward), and if not, how backward retrieval might necessitate additional processing to reorder items (Conrad, 1965; Thomas et al., 2003; see Donolato et al., 2017, for review).
text.formatted: Early research of this sort was motivated to test the proposal that recall was largely limited to the direction of encoding (i.e., forward), and if not, how backward retrieval might necessitate additional processing to reorder items <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Conrad, 1965;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Thomas et al., 2003</ref>; see <ref type="bibr">Donolato et al., 2017, for review)</ref>.

text.text: For the most part, these studies demonstrated that forward and backward recall are respectively associated with larger primacy and recency effects (e.g., Guitard et al., 2020; Hinrichs, 1968; Li and Lewandowsky, 1995), and that backward recall is overall slower and less accurate (e.g., Anders and Lillyquist, 1971; Bireta et al., 2010; Guérard et al., 2012; Surprenant et al., 2011; for exception, see Madigan, 1971), suggesting that retrieving in the two directions might be supported by qualitatively distinct processes.
text.formatted: For the most part, these studies demonstrated that forward and backward recall are respectively associated with larger primacy and recency effects (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Guitard et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Hinrichs, 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Li and Lewandowsky, 1995)</ref>, and that backward recall is overall slower and less accurate (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Anders and Lillyquist, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bireta et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Guérard et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Surprenant et al., 2011</ref>; for exception, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Madigan, 1971)</ref>, suggesting that retrieving in the two directions might be supported by qualitatively distinct processes.

text.text: One proposal is that forward recall largely depends on verbal processes, such as the formation and rehearsal of inter-item associations formed during encoding (Murdock, 1993), whereas backward recall relies to a greater extent on the use of processing and representation that is more visuospatially oriented (Li and Lewandowsky, 1995; St Clair-Thompson and Allen, 2013).
text.formatted: One proposal is that forward recall largely depends on verbal processes, such as the formation and rehearsal of inter-item associations formed during encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Murdock, 1993)</ref>, whereas backward recall relies to a greater extent on the use of processing and representation that is more visuospatially oriented <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Li and Lewandowsky, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">St Clair-Thompson and Allen, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Building on those ideas, Guitard and Saint-Aubin (2022; also see Guitard et al., 2020) combined dual-task procedures with whether or not subjects were provided foreknowledge about the serial recall direction prior to encoding.
text.formatted: Building on those ideas, Guitard and Saint-Aubin (2022; also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Guitard et al., 2020)</ref> combined dual-task procedures with whether or not subjects were provided foreknowledge about the serial recall direction prior to encoding.

text.text: By demonstrating a benefit for the match between processing at encoding and retrieval, as opposed to relying on a mixture of verbal and visuospatial processing in the absence of foreknowledge, their findings emphasize the use and adaptability of distinct processes in service of the direction of recall.
Free recall tasks have also been instrumental to understanding how memories are organized and subsequently retrieved according to time.

Even when instructed to freely recall items in any order, subjects often order their recall output based on the sequences of items at encoding, suggesting that retrieval relies at least in part on the formation of associations between multiple items or between an item and some correlate of time, such as list position or gradually-drifting context. Kahana and colleagues (e.g., Howard and Kahana, 2002; Kahana, 1996) have extensively investigated and modeled this temporal contiguity effect by quantifying the conditional response probability (CRP).
text.formatted: Even when instructed to freely recall items in any order, subjects often order their recall output based on the sequences of items at encoding, suggesting that retrieval relies at least in part on the formation of associations between multiple items or between an item and some correlate of time, such as list position or gradually-drifting context. <ref type="bibr">Kahana and colleagues (e.g., Howard and Kahana, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Kahana, 1996)</ref> have extensively investigated and modeled this temporal contiguity effect by quantifying the conditional response probability (CRP).

text.text: After recalling an item from a given list position, this measure indicates the probability of the item recalled next, conditionalized on its availability for report and the difference in positions of the two items (i.e., next minus previous position = lag).

Although the primary regularity in such recall patterns is that CRP decreases as the lag between successively recalled items increases, a secondary consistency is its directional asymmetry, whereby sequences of items recalled in the forward direction are more frequent than those in the backward direction.
A framework commonly put forth to account for this asymmetry involves multiple sources of context (i.e., temporal, spatial, and situational details) associated with each item.

Because presentation of an item on the study list will activate a combination of the item's list context (based on the preceding study items) and its pre-experimental context (from prior to the study list), the latter will also be included in the list context for subsequent study items, thus producing more forward transitions (for further discussion, see Kahana, 2020).
text.formatted: Because presentation of an item on the study list will activate a combination of the item's list context (based on the preceding study items) and its pre-experimental context (from prior to the study list), the latter will also be included in the list context for subsequent study items, thus producing more forward transitions (for further discussion, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Kahana, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Regardless of the interpretation, the asymmetry in free recall performance is consistent with that described previously for serial recall, again suggesting the possibility of distinct processes underlying forward versus backward retrieval.

Lastly, in addition to the wide use of the two procedures described above, studies employing cued recall are less frequent in addressing directional differences in list memory but contain design elements that are particularly relevant to the current study.

This procedure, sometimes referred to as the sequential probe technique, involves providing subjects with a cue (probe) item from a given list position and typically requiring them to recall the item that immediately followed (e.g., Posnansky, 1972; Woodward and Murdock, 1968; Woodward, 1970), with more recent studies extending the procedure to include backward transitions (e.g., Caplan et al., 2006; Kahana and Caplan, 2002).
text.formatted: This procedure, sometimes referred to as the sequential probe technique, involves providing subjects with a cue (probe) item from a given list position and typically requiring them to recall the item that immediately followed (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Posnansky, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Woodward and Murdock, 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Woodward, 1970)</ref>, with more recent studies extending the procedure to include backward transitions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Caplan et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Kahana and Caplan, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Kahana and Caplan (2002) demonstrated that, with short lists consisting of only three words (triplets) and with longer lists of 19 words, there were clear advantages in behavioral accuracy and response latency for forward compared to backward cued recall.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Kahana and Caplan (2002)</ref> demonstrated that, with short lists consisting of only three words (triplets) and with longer lists of 19 words, there were clear advantages in behavioral accuracy and response latency for forward compared to backward cued recall.

text.text: This distinction between directions is again consistent with the asymmetries present in serial and free recall.

Moreover, it contrasts with the symmetric (correlated) forward and backward cued recall effects usually observed for word item pairs (for review, see Kahana, 2002), supporting the notion that even the shortest list size (of three items) can elicit distinct processing in support of retrieval direction.
text.formatted: Moreover, it contrasts with the symmetric (correlated) forward and backward cued recall effects usually observed for word item pairs (for review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Kahana, 2002)</ref>, supporting the notion that even the shortest list size (of three items) can elicit distinct processing in support of retrieval direction.

text.text: Aside from the available behavioral evidence described above, further understanding the processes underlying the forward/backward distinction in retrieval could be gained from examining its neural correlates.
Several studies have used neural measures in conjunction with the various list recall paradigms outlined above (for review, see Donolato et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Several studies have used neural measures in conjunction with the various list recall paradigms outlined above (for review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Donolato et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, these studies have also employed a wide range of experimental manipulations, including different materials, list lengths, whether items were repeated or extensively rehearsed, and whether both or only one direction of recall was probed, making it difficult to extract much consistency in service of interpreting the findings.
Nevertheless, we provide some relevant examples here.

In one study that used the digit span task, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) indicated greater activity in occipital and prefrontal cortices associated with backward compared to forward recall (Sun et al., 2005).
text.formatted: In one study that used the digit span task, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) indicated greater activity in occipital and prefrontal cortices associated with backward compared to forward recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(Sun et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: These findings respectively suggest increased demands placed on visuospatial and controlled processing during backward recall, consistent with the behavioral results described above for serial recall and additionally with resting-state fMRI evidence linking activity in attentional and cognitive control networks with the backwards digit span test (Hausman et al., 2020; Li et al., 2012).
text.formatted: These findings respectively suggest increased demands placed on visuospatial and controlled processing during backward recall, consistent with the behavioral results described above for serial recall and additionally with resting-state fMRI evidence linking activity in attentional and cognitive control networks with the backwards digit span test <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Hausman et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Li et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In a line of research capitalizing on intracranial electroencephalographic (iEEG) measures in epileptic patients, oscillatory brain activity has been related to free recall of word lists.

These studies have demonstrated that high-frequency (~30-100 Hz; i.e., gamma band) oscillatory activity in lateral temporal and prefrontal cortices, as well as in the hippocampus, distinguishes whether recall was correct versus an intrusion in the period immediately preceding verbal report of those items (e.g., Burke et al., 2014; Long et al., 2017; Sederberg et al., 2007; also see Manning et al., 2011; Solomon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These studies have demonstrated that high-frequency (~30-100 Hz; i.e., gamma band) oscillatory activity in lateral temporal and prefrontal cortices, as well as in the hippocampus, distinguishes whether recall was correct versus an intrusion in the period immediately preceding verbal report of those items (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Burke et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Long et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Sederberg et al., 2007</ref>; also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Manning et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Solomon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Although these studies have exclusively been directed at understanding retrieval accuracy instead of its direction, their findings align with the extensive behavioral evidence suggesting that recall involves reinstating an item's study context which, in turn, activates other items associated with that context.

Two additional studies, using scalp EEG to investigate retrieval processes during free recall, are particularly noteworthy as they include analysis methods that motivate those adopted in the current study.

In an initial study, Katerman et al. (2022) attempted to identify neural correlates of free recall of words in the period of about 1.5 seconds immediately preceding verbal report (as in the iEEG studies noted above).
text.formatted: In an initial study, <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Katerman et al. (2022)</ref> attempted to identify neural correlates of free recall of words in the period of about 1.5 seconds immediately preceding verbal report (as in the iEEG studies noted above).

text.text: This period is thought to involve deliberation, search, and other related processes that eventually give rise to successful or unsuccessful recall but, importantly for the purposes of EEG analysis, is largely uncontaminated by artifact due to vocalization.

Consistent with the iEEG findings, Katerman et al. found that gamma-band (40-128 Hz) oscillatory power over posterior electrode sites increased in the moments leading up to the successful recall of a list word.

Additionally, this effect was elevated for delayed recall of words studied over multiple prior days compared to an immediate, one-item recall condition that allowed for control of pre-vocalization effects.
Analyses of power at lower frequencies also indicated differences, with increases in anterior theta (4-8 Hz) and widespread decreases in alpha (8-20 Hz) power preceding delayed recall.

Additionally, although the authors demonstrated that classifiers from encoding could predict subsequent temporal clustering of recalled words-i.e., successively recalling words from sequential study list positions, regardless of the direction of sequence-analogous effects were not evident from the recall-phase classifiers the scalp EEG data (but, for iEEG evidence, see Manning et al., 2011).

text.text: The current study was motivated, like the recent EEG studies just described, to further understand the neural basis of temporal organization at the time of memory retrieval.
Moreover, we were interested in addressing the novel question of whether such effects might relate to the forward-backward distinction and asymmetry observed across experimental paradigms.
Our study thus attempted to resolve some limitations of the behavioral procedures and neural analytic methods used previously.
First, we employed a recall task that explicitly and equitably probed list words in either the forward or backward direction (following Kahana and Caplan, 2002).
text.formatted: First, we employed a recall task that explicitly and equitably probed list words in either the forward or backward direction (following <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Kahana and Caplan, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: After studying lists of seven to nine words, our subjects completed an immediate cued recall task in which one word from the list was presented as a cue along with right-or left-ward symbols respectively indicating that the next or previous two list words should be reported.

This task was designed to overcome the infrequency of backward transitions usually found with free recall tasks (see Healey et al., 2019) and to mitigate the asymmetry often found with serial recall, whereby subjects respectively show strong primacy-and recency-dependent position curves for the forward and backward directions (Guitard et al., 2020; Li and Lewandowsky, 1995).
text.formatted: This task was designed to overcome the infrequency of backward transitions usually found with free recall tasks (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Healey et al., 2019)</ref> and to mitigate the asymmetry often found with serial recall, whereby subjects respectively show strong primacy-and recency-dependent position curves for the forward and backward directions <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Guitard et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Li and Lewandowsky, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: The second important feature of the current study was that MVPA was used in combination with the acquired scalp EEG data to contrast neural activity according to retrieval direction.

Although consistently shown to be more sensitive than traditional univariate methods at detecting subtle differences in fMRI activity between conditions (e.g., Cox and Savoy, 2003; Haxby et al., 2001; Kamitani and Tong, 2005), analogous MVPA approaches have been adapted more recently for EEG and magnetoencephalography (MEG) data (e.g., Carlson et al., 2011; Jafarpour et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2015;  for reviews and tutorials, see Grootswagers et al., 2017; King and Dehaene, 2014; Peelen and Downing, 2023).
text.formatted: Although consistently shown to be more sensitive than traditional univariate methods at detecting subtle differences in fMRI activity between conditions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cox and Savoy, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Haxby et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Kamitani and Tong, 2005)</ref>, analogous MVPA approaches have been adapted more recently for EEG and magnetoencephalography (MEG) data (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Carlson et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Jafarpour et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Johnson et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for reviews and tutorials, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Grootswagers et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">King and Dehaene, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Peelen and Downing, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As the current study is novel in investigating the EEG correlates of forward and backward retrieval, MVPA is especially suited to allow for exploring both eventrelated potential (ERP) and oscillatory (spectral) activity to identify distinguishing features that might engage widespread brain networks.

Additionally, our approach with this technique involves conducting individualsubject analyses, enabling the capture of any differences between conditions rather than requiring differences to be consistent across subjects (e.g., in terms of topography, spectral frequency, or direction of effect).

Finally, and not unrelated to the previous two features, we employed an extended (5-second) deliberation period with our cued recall task, ensuring that subjects had adequate time to actively engage in retrieval processing prior to being signaled to verbally report.

These long periods not only eliminate the variable and often shorter periods that typically precede report in free recall but also provide artifact-free data that enhances our ability to train MVPA classifiers to detect neural differences between forward and backward retrieval.
>METHODS
text.formatted: <head n="2." >METHODS</head>

text.text: Twenty-eight undergraduate students from the University of Missouri (MU) participated in partial fulfillment of credit for an introductory psychology course.
All subjects reported being right-handed, learning English as their first language, and having normal/corrected vision and no history of neurological disorders.
Informed consent was obtained in accordance with the MU Institutional Review Board.
Data from four subjects were excluded from all analyses: one due to technical errors with the EEG recording, one due to too much artifact in the EEG, and two for abnormal behavioral performance.

Of the latter two, one subject seemingly reported as many items as possible per study list (M = 3.88), compared to the ideal of two items, and the other usually reported only one item per list (M = 1.02).
The final sample of 24 subjects (16 women and 8 men) were between 18 and 22 years of age (M = 19).
The stimulus pool consisted of 1,000 common words from the Toronto Word Pool (Friendly et al., 1982; https://memory.psych.upenn.edu/Word_Pools).
text.formatted: The stimulus pool consisted of 1,000 common words from the Toronto Word Pool <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Friendly et al., 1982</ref>; <ref type="url" target="https://memory.psych.upenn.edu/Word_Pools">https://memory.psych.upenn.edu/Word_Pools</ref>).

text.text: The words were three to eight letters long (M = 6.25; SD = 1.00), had a mean imagery rating of 4.19 (1/low to 7/high; SD = 1.41), and a mean concreteness rating of 4.33 (1/abstract to 7/concrete; SD = 1.38).

Stimuli were displayed in white uppercase 36-point Arial font against the gray background of a 19" LCD monitor set to a resolution of 1024 × 768 pixels and viewed at a distance of approximately 80 cm.
Based on the screen size and resolution, the longest word was approximately 9 cm wide (with letters about 1 cm high).
Stimulus presentation, timing, and response acquisition were controlled by the PsychToolbox package (ver.
3.0.19; http://psychtoolbox.org/) in MATLAB (ver. 2024a; MathWorks, Natick, MA).
text.formatted: 3.0.19; <ref type="url" target="http://psychtoolbox.org/">http://psychtoolbox.org/</ref>) in MATLAB (ver. 2024a; MathWorks, Natick, MA).

text.text: Upon arriving at the laboratory, subjects were instructed about and completed practice versions of the experiment's tasks.
They were then prepared with an EEG cap and electrodes, which lasted approximately 30 minutes.
The total duration of the experimental session was about 2.5 hours.
Figure 1a provides a schematic of the experimental stimuli and task, along with some example response conditions.
The experiment consisted of 48 cycles of a study list followed immediately by a cued recall test.
Each study list involved visual presentation of 7, 8, or 9 randomly selected words from the stimulus pool.
Following an initial 'get ready' instruction presented centrally for 5 s, study words were displayed centrally for 2 s each.
A central fixation marker ('+') was shown during the interstimulus intervals for a jittered period of .8-1.2 s (randomly selected from a uniform distribution).
After the final word in a study list was displayed, there was a jittered delay of 1.2-1.4 s of fixation before a cue to be used for recall appeared on screen.

The cued recall task was directional in nature, consisting of one of the words from the preceding study list presented just above a row of either five greater than ('>>>>>') or less than ('<<<<<') symbols.
text.formatted: The cued recall task was directional in nature, consisting of one of the words from the preceding study list presented just above a row of either five greater than ('>>>>>') or less than ('<<<<<') symbols.

text.text: The symbols respectively indicated that subjects should attempt to recall words from the study list in the forward or backward direction, starting with the position of the presented cue word.

Only one recall cue was presented for each list, and cue words were randomly selected from all possible study positions, with the constraint that there were two words that could be recalled in the appropriate direction (i.e., the cue word for forward recall never came from the last two list positions, and the cue word for backward recall never came from the first two positions).

The word and symbols were displayed centrally for a 5-s deliberation period, while subjects were asked to search for and continually think about the next two or previous two words relative to the cued position.
A row of five question marks ('?????') was then shown centrally for 4 s, during which subjects were to verbally report the words they recalled.

Subjects were additionally instructed that, in the event that they were unsure about the next or previous two words or their exact order, they should report their best guess(es) or partial information, emphasizing that recalling words from the cued direction was most important.
Verbal responses were recorded to the stimulus presentation computer and were later manually transcribed by the first author.

Across the experimental session, there were eight study list/recall cycles for each combination of list length (7, 8, or 9 words) and cued recall direction (forward or backward), presented in a random order.
The processed EEG data, along with the corresponding behavioral data and relevant analysis code used for this study are available at https://osf.io/t6qea/.
text.formatted: The processed EEG data, along with the corresponding behavioral data and relevant analysis code used for this study are available at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/t6qea/">https://osf.io/t6qea/</ref>.

text.text: Other forms of data and study materials are available upon request to the authors.
EEG was acquired continuously across the entire session from a 64-channel BrainAmp Standard system (Brain Vision, LLC, Durham, NC; https://www.brainvision.com/).
text.formatted: EEG was acquired continuously across the entire session from a 64-channel BrainAmp Standard system (Brain Vision, LLC, Durham, NC; <ref type="url" target="https://www.brainvision.com/">https://www.brainvision.com</ref>).

text.text: Data were recorded at a bandwidth of .016 Hz (10-s time constant) to 1 kHz, a sampling rate of 1 kHz, and a resolution of .1 µV.

Electrode locations were based on the extended 10-20 system (Chatrian et al., 1985; Easycap montage 11, https://www.easycap.de/) and included the following sites: Fpz/1/2, AFz/3/4/7/8, Fz and F1-8, FC1-6, FT7/8, Cz and C1-6, T7/8, CPz and CP1-6, TP7/8, Pz and P1-8, POz/3/4/7/8, and O1/2.
text.formatted: Electrode locations were based on the extended 10-20 system <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chatrian et al., 1985</ref>; Easycap montage 11, <ref type="url" target="https://www.easycap.de/">https://www.easycap.de</ref>) and included the following sites: Fpz/1/2, AFz/3/4/7/8, Fz and F1-8, FC1-6, FT7/8, Cz and C1-6, T7/8, CPz and CP1-6, TP7/8, Pz and P1-8, POz/3/4/7/8, and O1/2.

text.text: Data were recorded with reference to an electrode placed at FCz (which was recovered during processing), and a ground electrode was placed at FT10.

Additional electrodes were placed on the mastoids (M1/2), below the left eye (IO1), and on the outer canthi (LO1/2), but these electrodes were removed from the dataset prior to processing and analysis.
Electrodes were adjusted until impedances were below 5 kΩ prior to the start of the experiment.
Because our hypotheses were based only on neural activity related to the cued recall task, the data acquired during the study lists are not reported on here.
Offline processing of the EEG data was completed with the EEGLAB toolbox (ver.
2024.2; Delorme and Makeig, 2004; https://sccn.ucsd.edu/eeglab/index.php) in MATLAB (ver. 2024a).
text.formatted: 2024.2; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Delorme and Makeig, 2004</ref>; <ref type="url" target="https://sccn.ucsd.edu/eeglab/index.php">https://sccn.ucsd.edu/eeglab/index.php</ref>) in MATLAB (ver. 2024a).

text.text: The data were first high-pass filtered at .5 Hz and re-referenced to the average across all channels.
The data were then epoched from -2 to 6 s relative to the onset of each retrieval cue.

This epoch length captured the entire 5-s period (0 to 5 s) during which subjects were to deliberate about the adjacent study words, plus a baseline period (-1 to 0 s) and additional temporal padding (1 s in each direction) to accommodate the time-frequency transformation (see below).

Epoching at this early stage was intended to reduce the influence of artifact-laden data, particularly due to verbalized responding, on later processing steps (e.g., independent components analysis, ICA).
Line noise (at 60 Hz and the harmonic of 120 Hz) was then removed using the cleanline function of EEGLAB.
Epochs and entire channels with too much artifact were next manually identified and removed.
Across subjects, an average of 2.17 channels (SD = 1.81, range = 0 to 6) and 4.54 trials (SD = 3.41, range = 0 to 12) were removed.
For the forward and backward recall conditions of interest, the average remaining trial numbers were respectively 21.83 (SD = 1.88 range = 18 to 24) and 21.63 (SD = 1.93, range = 17 to 24).
The data were then subject to ICA, with the number of resulting components equal to the number of remaining channels minus one due to re-referencing.
Components strongly (>80% confidence) classified as muscle or eye artifact, based on ICLabel (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019), were then automatically subtracted from the data.
text.formatted: Components strongly (>80% confidence) classified as muscle or eye artifact, based on ICLabel (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019), were then automatically subtracted from the data.

text.text: On average, 12.33 components (SD = 4.52, range = 3 to 20) were subtracted via this method.
Finally, the channels that were removed manually were interpolated and reintroduced into the dataset.

We conducted two sets of analyses of the EEG data, based on multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA; see Grootswagers et al., 2017; Treder, 2020), that separately utilized the ERP (voltage) amplitude and the oscillatory (spectral) power.
text.formatted: We conducted two sets of analyses of the EEG data, based on multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Grootswagers et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Treder, 2020)</ref>, that separately utilized the ERP (voltage) amplitude and the oscillatory (spectral) power.

text.text: Prior to the ERP analyses, the data were baseline-corrected by subtracting the average amplitude from the -1 to 0 s period (relative to the retrieval cue onset).

For the oscillatory analyses, the data were further processed using the FieldTrip toolbox (Oostenveld et al., 2011; https://www.fieldtriptoolbox.org/) in MATLAB (ver. 2024a), which involved first down-sampling the data to 250 Hz (to reduce subsequent computation time for MVPA) and then transforming the data with a multi-taper Hanning method in 1-Hz increments from 4 to 120 Hz (time-window size of 4/frequency).
text.formatted: For the oscillatory analyses, the data were further processed using the FieldTrip toolbox <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Oostenveld et al., 2011</ref>; <ref type="url" target="https://www.fieldtriptoolbox.org/">https://www.fieldtriptoolbox.org</ref>) in MATLAB (ver. 2024a), which involved first down-sampling the data to 250 Hz (to reduce subsequent computation time for MVPA) and then transforming the data with a multi-taper Hanning method in 1-Hz increments from 4 to 120 Hz (time-window size of 4/frequency).

text.text: The transformed data were baseline-corrected to the -1 to 0 s period by dividing the average power at each frequency.
The MVPA-Light toolbox (Treder, 2020; https://github.com/treder/MVPA-Light-Paper), along with custom MATLAB code, was used to conduct MVPA.
text.formatted: The MVPA-Light toolbox <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Treder, 2020</ref>; <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/treder/MVPA-Light-Paper">https://github.com/treder/MVPA-Light-Paper</ref>), along with custom MATLAB code, was used to conduct MVPA.

text.text: All classifications were carried out using Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), with the regularization (lambda) parameter estimated automatically for each fold, repetition, and subject (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004).
text.formatted: All classifications were carried out using Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), with the regularization (lambda) parameter estimated automatically for each fold, repetition, and subject <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Ledoit and Wolf, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Patterns were z-scored across features prior to classification.

Classifier performance was measured as area under the curve (AUC) in order to accommodate any imbalances in the number of patterns per condition (primarily due either to trial rejection based on EEG artifact or the random assignment of trials to folds).
AUC varies between 0 and 1, with chance performance at .5.

These general classification settings were used in combination with other, specific parameters to conduct three types of analyses: (i) collapsing over the entire 5-s retrieval cue deliberation period, (ii) using different sizes of time windows (bins) to identify time-resolved differences, and (iii) characterizing the features (time bins and frequency bands) important to the classification.
The details of these analyses are described in turn below, and their outcomes are reported in the same order in the Results (see section 3.2.).
For the first classification analyses that collapsed over the 5-s deliberation period, all trials (maximum of 24 per forward and backward conditions) were submitted to 5-fold cross-validation.
In this procedure, the trials from each condition were randomly split into five sets, with each set iteratively serving to test the classifier while the other four sets were used for training.
This procedure was then repeated five times, with the results averaged across iterations and repetitions.
The second set of classification analyses included time as a feature and used a two-step approach.
In the first step, we determined whether there was an optimal size of time bin for identifying distinct forward vs. backward patterns.
The ERP and oscillatory data across the 5-second epoch were thus binned into incrementally smaller bin sizes: 5, 2.5, 1, .5, .25, .1, .05, and .025 s.
Importantly, so as not to bias the results, the selection of bin size was determined via cross-validation on only half the data (odd trials from each condition).
Given the decrease in trial numbers used for this first step, 2-fold cross-validation was used, in which the trials were randomly assigned to the two folds.
This procedure was then repeated 10 times, and the classifier results were averaged across repetitions and folds.

In the second step, the optimal bin size (.025-s, to preview the results) was carried forward to train a final classifier on all of the odd trials from each condition and test the classifier on the remaining data (even trials from each condition).
For the last type of analyses, we sought to further characterize the time course and frequency bands that were driving the classifications.

These analyses made further use of the data binned into .025-s segments, but instead of using time merely as a feature, tracked classifier performance for the ERP and oscillatory patterns in two ways.
The time courses of neural differences were constructed for ERP and oscillatory patterns in parallel by cycling the classification procedure across successive time bins.

To additionally characterize the frequency bands involved in classifying oscillatory activity, the classification procedure was cycled over each combination of time (.025-s bins) and frequency (in 1-Hz increments).

Due to the number of separate classifications required for these analyses, we took the approach involved in the final classification of time (as described above), where individual classifiers were trained on the odd trials from each condition and tested on the even trials from each condition (i.e., k-fold cross-validation was not implemented).

For all analyses involving multiple statistical tests across non-independent data points, cluster-based Monte Carlo simulations were implemented to correct for multiple comparisons (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
text.formatted: For all analyses involving multiple statistical tests across non-independent data points, cluster-based Monte Carlo simulations were implemented to correct for multiple comparisons <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Maris and Oostenveld, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For the time course analyses, individual cluster-wise statistics correspond to the summed t-values (hereafter, tsum) over clustered (i.e., consecutively significant) time points (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
text.formatted: For the time course analyses, individual cluster-wise statistics correspond to the summed t-values (hereafter, tsum) over clustered (i.e., consecutively significant) time points <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Maris and Oostenveld, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For the time-frequency analyses, cluster-wise statistics (tsum) were determined across both the time and frequency dimensions.
Each simulation involved 1000 randomly-shuffled permutations of the condition labels.
The alpha level for individual data points was set to .05 and, as with the previous analyses of AUC, the group-level statistical tests were one-tailed against the chance level of .5.
The resulting p-values reported in the Results (see section 3.2.) correspond to the proportion of larger clusters (based on tsum) from the permutation-based null distribution.
To summarize the individual features contributing to the foregoing classifications, the trained classifier weights were extracted.
Our implementation of LDA results in a single weight value associated with each feature (also see Blankertz et al., 2011; Treder, 2020).
text.formatted: Our implementation of LDA results in a single weight value associated with each feature (also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Blankertz et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Treder, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: To allow for description of the sign and magnitude of the weights at the group level, each subject's weights were standardized into t-values (vs. a weight of 0).
We emphasize that the resulting weights are presented here purely for descriptive purposes for two reasons.
First, similarity across subjects in feature values is not a requirement for classification success.
That is, each subject's data were classified independently given that there might be variation in how subjects differentially process the forward and backward conditions.
Second, there is no need for the weights of adjacent features (e.g., nearby electrodes for ERP data, or nearby electrodes or frequency bands for the oscillatory data) to be correlated.
Therefore, we did not apply any cluster-correction procedures to these descriptive results.
>RESULTS  >Behavioral performance
text.formatted: <head n="3." >RESULTS</head> <head n="3.1." >Behavioral performance</head>

text.text: Analysis of the behavioral data first assessed overall performance on the cued recall task.

Following each study list, subjects were instructed to recall and verbally report two words from the list, either in the forward or backward direction, relative to the position of a provided cue word (see Figure 1a).
text.formatted: Following each study list, subjects were instructed to recall and verbally report two words from the list, either in the forward or backward direction, relative to the position of a provided cue word (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: If both words could not be recalled, subjects were to report partial information or make their best guess, with the instructions emphasizing the report of words from the cued direction (which was most relevant to the EEG classification analyses).
As shown in Figure 2b, against the ideal of two words reported per list, the average number of all words reported differed significantly at 2.25 (SD = .46; t23 = 2.65, p = .014).
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">2b</ref>, against the ideal of two words reported per list, the average number of all words reported differed significantly at 2.25 (SD = .46; t23 = 2.65, p = .014).

text.text: The behavioral data were next segregated according to accuracy.

Although there are numerous ways to consider recall accuracy, we took an approach here focusing on the instructional emphasis of whether words were correctly reported from the cued direction (i.e., previous words in the list for backward recall and subsequent words in the list for forward recall), regardless of the strict order of report or adherence to only the two words directly adjacent to the cue.

For example, if cued with the word from the third list position and in the forward direction, whereas the ideal response would be the fourth and then fifth words, our criterion for being correct also included reporting the fifth then fourth words, as well as reporting the fifth then seventh words.
Figure 1a provides some additional examples of possible responses and their corresponding condition labels.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref> provides some additional examples of possible responses and their corresponding condition labels.

text.text: Recall performance according to whether words were reported from the cued (correct) direction, from the uncued (incorrect) direction, or not from the current list at all (i.e., extra-list intrusions) is summarized in Figure 1b.
text.formatted: Recall performance according to whether words were reported from the cued (correct) direction, from the uncued (incorrect) direction, or not from the current list at all (i.e., extra-list intrusions) is summarized in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>.

text.text: As is apparent, words from the cued direction (M = 1.64, SD = 0.39) considerably exceeded those from the uncued direction (M = 0.26, SD = 0.15) and intrusions (M = 0.30, SD = 0.22).

To statistically test whether performance differed across the accuracy categories described above or with respect to the experimental manipulations, the measures were submitted to a three-way ANOVA including factors of accuracy category (cued direction, uncued direction, or intrusion), recall direction (forward or backward), and study list length (7, 8, or 9 words).

As expected, there was a significant main effect of accuracy category (F1.41,32.35 = 193.90, p < .001; fractional dfs correspond to Greenhouse-Geisser correction), with recall in the cued direction exceeding both that in the uncued direction (t23 = 14.48, p < .001) and intrusions (t23 = 15.25, p < .001), whereas the latter two categories did not differ (t23 = .67, p = .51).

text.text: Given the importance of equating the forward and backward conditions (see Introduction), Figure 1c provides the measures for each accuracy category according to this distinction.
text.formatted: Given the importance of equating the forward and backward conditions (see Introduction), Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref> provides the measures for each accuracy category according to this distinction.

text.text: As is apparent from the figure, responding was comparable for forward and backward recall, with the ANOVA revealing no significant effects involving the recall direction factor (all Fs < 1, except the recall direction × list length interaction, F1.61,37.12 = 2.75, p = .087).

text.text: Additionally, no other significant effects involving the list length or accuracy category factors were observed (all Fs < 1, except the accuracy category × list length interaction, F2.37,54.43 = 1.39, p = .26).
text.formatted: Additionally, no other significant effects involving the list length or accuracy category factors were observed (all Fs < 1, except the accuracy category × list length interaction, F2.37,54.43 = 1.39, p = .26).

text.text: To further facilitate comparison of performance in our directional cued recall task with the findings of other investigations of directional retrieval, the behavioral data were next examined with respect to serial position and lag effects.

Figure 2 displays the proportions of correctly reporting a word from a particular serial position, given that the position was one of the two cued for subjects to report, separated by recall direction and list length.

text.text: To test for any systematic effects across serial position, we simplified the list length manipulation by collapsing positions into three bins-early (first two positions), late (last two positions), and middle (the remaining positions, which differed according to list length)-as is shown in Figure 2d.

The primary goal of the EEG classification analyses was to determine whether patterns of neural activity could provide novel evidence that retrieval deliberation and search were distinguishable between the forward versus backward directions.
To this end, the EEG was classified in a series of analyses that used, in parallel, either ERP (voltage) amplitude or oscillatory (spectral) power.
First, we collapsed these data across the entire retrieval cue deliberation period, under the assumption that processing in service of retrieval direction was continually maintained during this time.
Next, in case differential processing varied across time (as opposed to being engaged consistently), the analyses turned to including time as an additional classification feature.

Finally, we cycled the classification procedure across specific time bins and frequency bands, allowing for characterization of features in the EEG data that could potentially inform subsequent research on directional retrieval processing while also ensuring the reliability of our effects according to cluster-based statistical correction.

Given that subjects were instructed to deliberate about retrieval throughout the 5-s period in which the word and direction cues were presented, the classification analyses were initially conducted on the EEG data averaged over this period.

While classified ERP patterns consisted of 60 features (voltage amplitude at each electrode), oscillatory patterns comprised 7,020 features (spectral power from 4 to 120 Hz in 1-Hz increments × 60 electrodes).
As shown in Figure 4a, mean performance (AUC) of the resulting ERP classifier was numerically below chance at .48 (SD = .082; t23 = -1.41, p = .91).

text.text: (Note that one-tailed statistical tests were used when contrasting AUC against chance, given the alternative hypothesis that any discriminable information between conditions should increase classifier performance.)

Despite the forward and backward conditions being indistinguishable based on averaged ERP data, classifying the oscillatory data resulted in a mean AUC of .54 (SD = .097; also see Figure 4a), which significantly exceeded the chance level (t23 = 2.26, p = .017).

text.text: Directly comparing the performance of the ERP-and oscillation-based classifiers also revealed a significant difference (t23 = 2.27, p = .033).

The preceding analyses indicated that classifying the EEG data collapsed over time, while giving rise to significant above-chance performance for the oscillatory data, still resulted in accuracy levels that were near or below chance for several subjects.

One possible reason for this limit on observed classification performance is that, rather than being engaged consistently throughout the 5-s deliberation period, the neural processes differentiating the forward and backward conditions fluctuated across time.
The next analyses thus examined whether time carried information important to retrieval direction by including it as an additional classification feature.

Using time as a feature involved a two-step approach in which an optimal time bin size was first selected via cross-validation on half of the data and then a final classifier was evaluated on the remaining, untouched half of the data (see section 2.5. for further details).
Figure 4b summarizes the results of the first step for the ERP and oscillatory data across a range of bin sizes: 5, 2.5, 1, .5, .25, .1, .05, and .025 s.

For the oscillatory classification, the results were less clear, with AUC values overall being closer to chance and having a maximum value of .51 (SD = .13, t23 = .40, p = .35) at the .025-s bin size.

Note that it is unsurprising that performance for the previous classifications (see Figure 4a) is less noisy than that reported here when time is a feature, since the latter is based on classifying only half of the available data (odd trials from each condition).

As described in the Introduction (see section 1.), numerous studies using different list-memory paradigms have shown that the temporal sequence of events during memory encoding can influence how those events are later retrieved.

The underlying neural correlates of retrieving sequences of memories, and in particular whether forward and backward retrieval processes can be neurally distinguished, remain to be elucidated, in part due to consistent evidence that backward retrieval search is considerably less frequent and is usually associated with worse behavioral performance than forward search (e.g., Guitard et al., 2020 Guitard et al., , 2022;; Kahana, 1996; Kahana and Caplan, 2002; Murdock, 1968; but see Madigan, 1971).
text.formatted: The underlying neural correlates of retrieving sequences of memories, and in particular whether forward and backward retrieval processes can be neurally distinguished, remain to be elucidated, in part due to consistent evidence that backward retrieval search is considerably less frequent and is usually associated with worse behavioral performance than forward search (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Guitard et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Guitard et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Kahana, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Kahana and Caplan, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Murdock, 1968</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Madigan, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we employed an experimental procedure that attempted to equate behavior across retrieval direction so that EEG data could be used to characterize any differences in neural processing.

After studying lists of about eight successively presented words, subjects undertook an immediate, directional cued recall task in which they were instructed to recall two list words by moving either forward or backward relative to the provided cue.
The behavioral results indicated success of the task's primary goal, in that subjects were able to report the desired number of recalled items.

Additionally, across both the forward and backward conditions, correct recall in the cued direction substantially exceeded incorrect recall in the uncued direction as well as the report of extra-list intrusions.
Our behavioral results further aligned with findings widely observed in the literature on list memory.

Namely, we found differences in behavioral accuracy according to serial position, where performance was better for words from the early and late list positions compared to those from the middle (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: Namely, we found differences in behavioral accuracy according to serial position, where performance was better for words from the early and late list positions compared to those from the middle (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: These findings are consistent with serial position effects that have been shown in both serial and free recall tasks (e.g., Deese and Kaufman, 1957; Howard and Kahana, 1999; Jahnke, 1965; Murdock, 1962; Ward et al., 2010).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with serial position effects that have been shown in both serial and free recall tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Deese and Kaufman, 1957;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Howard and Kahana, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Jahnke, 1965;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Murdock, 1962;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Ward et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, lag-based analyses of our cued recall data, employing the conditional response probability (CRP) measure routinely used in studies of free recall (e.g., Kahana, 1996; for review, see Healey et al., 2019; but see Farrell and Lewandowsky, 2008, for limitations), revealed that words nearer to the cued position were recalled at higher rates than those more distant.
text.formatted: Additionally, lag-based analyses of our cued recall data, employing the conditional response probability (CRP) measure routinely used in studies of free recall (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Kahana, 1996</ref>; for review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Healey et al., 2019</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Farrell and Lewandowsky, 2008</ref>, for limitations), revealed that words nearer to the cued position were recalled at higher rates than those more distant.

text.text: Importantly, considering the current results in the context of these position and lag effects indicated that subjects were able to successfully retrieve memories in both directions and, moreover, did so with equivalent performance across direction.

Taken together, these behavioral findings meet the prerequisite to be able to use the corresponding EEG data to distinguish brain activity on the basis of potentially qualitatively-distinct directional retrieval processes as opposed to being conflated by other, generally less interesting factors such as task difficulty, effort, or whether the outcome of the retrieval search was successful.

Turning to the EEG findings, our use of MVPA was able to sensitively detect neural activity patterns that differed between the forward and backward conditions and were presumably a reflection of the distinct deliberation and search processes that served the two directions of recall.

This approach was largely exploratory given the lack of existing studies that contrasted directional retrieval in list-learning paradigms, particular with EEG (cf. Hoshi et al., 2000; Sun et al., 2005).
text.formatted: This approach was largely exploratory given the lack of existing studies that contrasted directional retrieval in list-learning paradigms, particular with EEG (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Hoshi et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Sun et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Borrowing from recent studies employing scalp EEG to investigate neural activity just prior to verbal report in free recall tasks (Katerman et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024), our analyses focused on a 5-second period that preceded recall vocalization, allowing for assessment of retrieval-related processes while minimizing artifacts in the EEG due to vocalization.
text.formatted: Borrowing from recent studies employing scalp EEG to investigate neural activity just prior to verbal report in free recall tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Katerman et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Li et al., 2024)</ref>, our analyses focused on a 5-second period that preceded recall vocalization, allowing for assessment of retrieval-related processes while minimizing artifacts in the EEG due to vocalization.

text.text: Additionally, our cued recall procedure ensured adequate numbers of trials per directional retrieval condition to allow for balanced classifier training, contrasting with the imbalance between forward and backward list transitions often observed in free recall.
To this end, the present analyses produced multiple results differentiating the two conditions, some of which are highlighted here for further discussion.

First, parallel analyses directed at classifying ERP amplitude and oscillatory activity demonstrated that only the latter consistently gave rise to accuracy levels that significantly exceeded chance (but see, e.g., Carlson et al., 2011, and Johnson et al., 2015, for positive results with ERP data).
text.formatted: First, parallel analyses directed at classifying ERP amplitude and oscillatory activity demonstrated that only the latter consistently gave rise to accuracy levels that significantly exceeded chance (but see, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Carlson et al., 2011, and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Johnson et al., 2015,</ref> for positive results with ERP data).

text.text: This difference according to data type was evident regardless of whether the data were averaged over the entire deliberation period, or when time (.025-s bins) was involved, either as an additional classier feature or to construct the time courses of classification performance.
The advantage for oscillatory activity, although notably not always significant by direct comparison with the ERP-based results, could be attributed to a number of factors.

On the more interesting side, these might include the inherent insensitivity of ERPs to higher-frequency and non-phase-locked neural activity (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006; also see Solomon et al., 2017), but it is also difficult to rule out the fact that better classifier performance might merely be due to the increased number of features (i.e., the amount of information) available in the oscillatory data.

text.text: The second set of results from the EEG analyses providing further characterization of the differences between forward and backward recall notably demonstrated that the effects were transient as well as restricted in terms of frequency signature.

That is, in analyzing the time course of classification, above-chance accuracy was not sustained throughout the deliberation period but was instead present at just two short latency clusters, beginning at about .7 and 2.3 seconds following cue onset and lasting around .1 second in each case (see Figure 5b).

text.text: Additionally, analyses localizing activity simultaneously across both time and frequency further confirmed the reliability of the late effect, with accuracy exceeding chance across portions of both the low-and high-gamma bands (from around 50-100 Hz; see Figure 6b).

text.text: The current results thus extend those of recent studies that have examined oscillatory signatures of retrieval accuracy in free recall.

In particular, increases in posteriorlymaximal gamma power have been previously shown during the deliberation period leading up to successful recall (compared to intrusions) with both scalp EEG (Katerman et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024) and intracranial EEG (e.g., Burke et al., 2014; Sederberg et al., 2007; Long et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In particular, increases in posteriorlymaximal gamma power have been previously shown during the deliberation period leading up to successful recall (compared to intrusions) with both scalp EEG <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Katerman et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Li et al., 2024)</ref> and intracranial EEG (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Burke et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Sederberg et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Long et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that such high-frequency activity might be predominantly related to forward transitions (which, as we have discussed, are more frequent in free recall) and potentially modulated further by the direction of retrieval.

We note, however, that any relationship between the role of gamma-band activity for our directional manipulation and that for retrieval success is only speculative and should await examination of both effects in the same experimental paradigm.

As noted in the Introduction (see section 1.), Katerman et al. (2022) also demonstrated an increase in theta power alongside a decrease in alpha power associated with free recall, with Li et al. (2024) subsequently confirming the alpha suppression effect with MVPA of scalp EEG.
