(2022)</ref> also demonstrated an increase in theta power alongside a decrease in alpha power associated with free recall, with <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Li et al. (2024)</ref> subsequently confirming the alpha suppression effect with MVPA of scalp EEG.

text.text: Distinct from those prior findings is the absence of such effects in the current study, which might be attributable to any number of differences or limitations of our design and analyses.

For instance, we were unable to contrast neural activity according to recall accuracy, given that both intrusions and recalls in the uncued (incorrect) direction were relatively rare (combined, about a third as likely correct recalls).

This leaves open the possibility that, although there is some discrepancy in the literature relating theta power increases versus decreases to episodic memory (e.g., Long and Kuhl, 2019; Osipova et al., 2006; for review, see Herweg et al., 2020), increases in theta might be more sensitive to successful retrieval or a mechanism that correlates with it, such as binding or reactivation (for reviews, see Hanslmayr et al., 2012; Nyhus and Curran, 2010).
text.formatted: This leaves open the possibility that, although there is some discrepancy in the literature relating theta power increases versus decreases to episodic memory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Long and Kuhl, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Osipova et al., 2006</ref>; for review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Herweg et al., 2020)</ref>, increases in theta might be more sensitive to successful retrieval or a mechanism that correlates with it, such as binding or reactivation (for reviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Hanslmayr et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Nyhus and Curran, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As the current results indicate, activity in the theta band might not be related to retrieval direction, especially when accuracy is equated across direction.

Additionally, under the assumption that decreased alpha power is often correlated with task engagement or readiness (Griffiths et al., 2021; ; Hanslmayr et al., 2007; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996; also see Klimesch, 1997), it is possible that the extended duration and fixed timing of our deliberation periods mitigated any trial-by-trial differences in engagement.
text.formatted: Additionally, under the assumption that decreased alpha power is often correlated with task engagement or readiness <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Griffiths et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hanslmayr et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Pfurtscheller et al., 1996</ref>; also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Klimesch, 1997)</ref>, it is possible that the extended duration and fixed timing of our deliberation periods mitigated any trial-by-trial differences in engagement.

text.text: By contrast, it could be argued that subjects exhibit larger fluctuations in states of alertness or readiness in tasks such as free recall (and even recognition), where items might be self-generated (or tested) more rapidly and with more variation in retrieval success.

Finally, while the extended (5-second) period prior to recall report in our task was designed to allow for continuous retrieval deliberation, and ideally isolate it from other cognitive processes, analogous to methods that have been successfully employed with MVPA in studies of working memory (e.g., Ester et al., 2015; LaRocque et al., 2013; Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012), the free recall studies of Katerman et al. (2022) and Li et al. (2024) analyzed much shorter periods of about one second or less.
text.formatted: Finally, while the extended (5-second) period prior to recall report in our task was designed to allow for continuous retrieval deliberation, and ideally isolate it from other cognitive processes, analogous to methods that have been successfully employed with MVPA in studies of working memory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Ester et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">LaRocque et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012)</ref>, the free recall studies of <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Katerman et al. (2022)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Li et al. (2024)</ref> analyzed much shorter periods of about one second or less.

text.text: Our long deliberation period thus might have included differential processing for forward vs. backward retrieval, but it was present in a transient or unpredictable manner, therefore weakening our ability to detect some of the difference.
An obvious next step would be to shorten the deliberation period while still ensuring the minimization of artifact in the EEG due to verbal report.

In terms of further interpreting the neural differences observed here between forward and backward retrieval, it is potentially helpful to turn to one of the largely-invariant characteristics of the CRP: forward asymmetry.

Even simple chaining models of memory have addressed this effect, positing that associations are formed between successive items in a list, and that forward associations are typically stronger than backward ones (Murdock, 1993; Raskin and Cook, 1937; Solway et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Even simple chaining models of memory have addressed this effect, positing that associations are formed between successive items in a list, and that forward associations are typically stronger than backward ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Murdock, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Raskin and Cook, 1937;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Solway et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, our results could reflect this difference in associative strength according to direction or, perhaps secondarily, subjects' attempts to overcome the difficulty with backward associations during the deliberation period (but notably doing so as to give rise to equivalent performance with forward retrieval by the end of the period).

More recently, memory models that incorporate context as a central feature, such as the retrieved context theory (Howard and Kahana, 2002; for review, see Kahana, 2020), have proposed that the temporal contiguity effect occurs not only due to item-item associations but also as a result of an automatic process of forming reciprocal bonds between items and their presentation context.
text.formatted: More recently, memory models that incorporate context as a central feature, such as the retrieved context theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Howard and Kahana, 2002</ref>; for review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Kahana, 2020)</ref>, have proposed that the temporal contiguity effect occurs not only due to item-item associations but also as a result of an automatic process of forming reciprocal bonds between items and their presentation context.

text.text: The forward asymmetry, as a result, can then be attributed to the encoding of a particular item based on the context created by just-presented items, which would not occur as strongly in the opposite (backward) direction.

The effects we observed in the gamma band could thus reflect cortical activity associated with differences in hippocampally-mediated contextual reinstatement-an interpretation consistent with the memoryrelated interactions that have been observed between theta and gamma oscillations (e.g., Düzel et al., 2003; Koster et al., 2014; Mormann et al., 2005) and which might contribute to the ordering of episodic memories (Jensen and Colgin, 2007; Lisman, 2005; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; also see Nyhus and Curran, 2010).
text.formatted: The effects we observed in the gamma band could thus reflect cortical activity associated with differences in hippocampally-mediated contextual reinstatement-an interpretation consistent with the memoryrelated interactions that have been observed between theta and gamma oscillations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Düzel et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Koster et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Mormann et al., 2005)</ref> and which might contribute to the ordering of episodic memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Jensen and Colgin, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Lisman, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Lisman and Jensen, 2013</ref>; also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Nyhus and Curran, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As we noted above, though, contrary to this account is our failure to observe theta differences, possibly due to these effects being limited to deep structures like the hippocampus and difficult to detect with scalp measures.

Considering the broader implications of our findings, there is a growing body of research contrasting the retrieval of past events and the simulation (or imagination) of future events (for reviews, see Schacter et al., 2012; Addis, 2020) to further understand the theoretical concept of mental time travel (MTT; Tulving, 1985 Tulving, , 2002)).
text.formatted: Considering the broader implications of our findings, there is a growing body of research contrasting the retrieval of past events and the simulation (or imagination) of future events (for reviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Schacter et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Addis, 2020)</ref> to further understand the theoretical concept of mental time travel (MTT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Tulving, 1985</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Tulving, , 2002))</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, a subset of those studies has investigated the past and future at a more specific, or granular, level, which might be more analogous to the inter-item transitions we tested in the current study.

For instance, Arzy et al. (2008 Arzy et al. ( , 2009) ) had subjects project themselves to different landmark time points in the past or future (i.e., 10 years in either direction) and then decide whether a particular personal or historical event had already occurred or was yet to happen.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Arzy et al. (2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Arzy et al. ( , 2009) )</ref> had subjects project themselves to different landmark time points in the past or future (i.e., 10 years in either direction) and then decide whether a particular personal or historical event had already occurred or was yet to happen.

text.text: By setting such landmarks, a distinction could be made between absolute (past versus future) and relative (before or after the landmark) MTT.

In addition to observing better behavioral performance (faster RTs and higher accuracy) for events nearer to compared to more distant from the present (also see Addis et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007), performance was better in the relative future (i.e., forward) than the relative past (i.e., backward) direction.
text.formatted: In addition to observing better behavioral performance (faster RTs and higher accuracy) for events nearer to compared to more distant from the present (also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Addis et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Szpunar et al., 2007)</ref>, performance was better in the relative future (i.e., forward) than the relative past (i.e., backward) direction.

text.text: On the surface, those findings appear consistent with the forward asymmetry commonly observed in list memory studies but successfully mitigated by the procedure of the current study.

Perhaps more interesting, however, are the scalp EEG correlates observed by Arzy et al. (2008), in which effects localized to lateral temporal and inferior frontal and parietal scalp were engaged for shorter durations in the relative future compared to relative past events.
text.formatted: Perhaps more interesting, however, are the scalp EEG correlates observed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Arzy et al. (2008)</ref>, in which effects localized to lateral temporal and inferior frontal and parietal scalp were engaged for shorter durations in the relative future compared to relative past events.

text.text: Despite the confound in difficulty, these results again leave open the possibility that directional retrieval engages distinct processing, consistent with the numerous behavioral findings from serial, free, and cued recall (as outlined in the Introduction).

A beneficial path for future research would be to bring together the granular, item-based transitions involved in list memory with the longer-term transitions of personal and real-world events (which were on the order of years in Arzy et al., 2008 Arzy et al., , 2009)).
text.formatted: A beneficial path for future research would be to bring together the granular, item-based transitions involved in list memory with the longer-term transitions of personal and real-world events (which were on the order of years in <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Arzy et al., 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Arzy et al., , 2009))</ref>.

text.text: To conclude, the findings presented here extend those of recent studies using scalp EEG to understand the neural activity preceding successful memory recall (Katerman et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024) and provide further evidence that retrieval processing is guided by temporal organization.
text.formatted: To conclude, the findings presented here extend those of recent studies using scalp EEG to understand the neural activity preceding successful memory recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Katerman et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Li et al., 2024)</ref> and provide further evidence that retrieval processing is guided by temporal organization.

text.text: Specifically, using a procedure that explicitly cued subjects to move either forward or backward over a memory list, we were able to not only replicate classic effects of serial position and recall contiguity but also equate behavioral performance across conditions.

In doing so, the distinct patterns of high-frequency (gamma-band) oscillatory activity observed for forward and backward retrieval can confidently be attributed to deliberation and search processes engaged differently according to temporal direction, as opposed to other confounding factors (e.g., difficulty or retrieval outcome).
